assumptions: The initial offer is limited to professional counterparties and does not rely on direct consumer resale.
All regulated collection, storage, transport, preparation for reuse, dismantling, battery handling, and formal testing are performed by appropriately authorized and insured partners.
The founder can use the family installation company for a bounded pilot, but that access does not imply that unrelated installers will grant equivalent rights.
No removal volume, reusable share, price, margin, return rate, partner quote, buyer commitment, or first-refusal agreement is treated as validated beyond the supplied evidence.
The business must remain operable within the founder's part-time limit and initial capital constraints until objective traction justifies a change in commitment.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The strongest insight is that value and legal optionality may be captured upstream, at first notice of deinstallation and before ambiguous equipment is mishandled or routed as waste, rather than by building another recycler or marketplace. Combining title evidence, serial-level condition records, classification discipline, and conditional first refusal is a coherent control-point thesis. It remains a thesis because the scarcity and assignability of those source rights have not been demonstrated.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: The supplied law supports real compliance and documentation burdens, and uncertain residual value can create disposal friction for installers and owners. However, no buyer has accepted the proposed service, no installer has agreed to pay or transfer rights, and existing producer-responsibility, collection, and resale channels may already resolve enough of the problem. The absence of validation is treated as uncertainty, while the split between the compliance beneficiary, asset owner, and resale buyer is a structural obstacle to clear willingness to pay.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: An outsourced, no-speculative-inventory model can limit capital exposure and create both service-fee and success-fee revenue. Against that, every important driver is unknown: removal volume, reusable share, realized price, licensed testing and handling cost, sale-through time, returns, warranty allocation, CAC, repeat behavior, and owner earnings. Evidence that treatment is high-volume and low-return, together with live low-value inventory, makes the conjunction of pickup, testing, packaging, compliance, and downstream fees a genuine margin problem rather than merely missing validation. The supplied material does not yet support a plausible path to the founder's wealth objective.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: The family installer offers a concrete, low-cost pilot source in a bounded region, and rising PV waste and reuse activity suggests a nontrivial flow over time. The proposed beachhead is still too broad across equipment classes, triggers, conditions, payers, and buyer types; modules, inverters, and batteries have materially different value densities and compliance burdens. No sourced local removal volume or economically reusable share establishes that the first segment is large and dense enough.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Exclusive or preferential deinstallation rights could establish a defensible local supply position if they are durable and cover meaningful volume. None are signed, installers can use alternative routes, and established operators already span compliance, collection, testing, repair, resale, logistics, and recycling. The candidate identifies a potentially distinct upstream position but has not shown why incumbents or large installers could not add it or why a new intermediary could dominate a meaningful beachhead.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A proven intake, title, grading, and routing system could extend from one installer cluster to other regions, renewable-equipment classes, insurers, service networks, and professional buyers. Expansion would not be frictionless: each product class has different safety, testing, residual-value, waste-status, and partner requirements, while geographic growth can reduce route density. The adjacency map is credible but depends on first proving one narrow profitable flow.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Long-term exclusive supply contracts, serialized disposition histories, buyer-demand data, and route density could reinforce one another. At present those assets do not exist, the proposed rights are conditional rather than demonstrably exclusive, and much of the workflow can be replicated using the same licensed partners. Established downstream operators have both strategic incentive and capability to integrate upstream, so durability depends on contract quality and local density that remain unproven.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A single documented route from removal decision to lawful disposition could be more convenient and safer than ad hoc handling, while recovering upside where equipment remains a product. There is no measured improvement in installer cost, turnaround, recovery value, liability, or buyer trust versus existing operators. Because regulated custody and technical work are outsourced, the venture risks becoming a thin coordination layer without a sufficiently large or exclusive advantage.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Growing PV waste and reuse activity, an aging installed base, and stringent EU documentation and safety duties create a timely need for better classification and routing. Weak international guidance for second-hand PV leaves room for trusted operating standards and data. The same uncertainty raises testing and liability costs, and incumbents are already active, so timing is favorable but not an uncontested window.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The family installer is an unusually practical zero-to-low-CAC starting channel and can expose real removals without broad cold outreach. Professional marketplaces and licensed partners provide reachable downstream channels. Beyond the pilot, acquiring recurring first-notice and first-refusal agreements is relationship-heavy, removal events are episodic, and no evidence establishes repeatable installer acquisition, contractual exclusivity, or dense supply, so the initial edge has not yet become a scalable channel.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's data and automation skills fit serial-level triage, and outsourcing regulated physical operations reduces capital and credential demands. Execution still requires a precise Polish legal and permit map, dependable licensed partners, title verification, insurance, safety and warranty allocation, exception handling, buyer disputes, and economically coordinated logistics. These are obtainable capabilities rather than direct fatal evidence, but managing them part-time across multiple equipment classes would be difficult until the workflow is narrowed and standardized.

main_structural_strength: An upstream first-notice and conditional first-refusal position, seeded through the family installer and coupled to serial-level evidence, could control valuable supply optionality while authorized partners carry regulated physical operations.
primary_score_limiter: There is no evidence that recoverable value plus a service fee consistently exceeds the full compliant cost of acquisition, classification, testing, logistics, returns, and partner margins, nor that installers will grant the source rights needed at sufficient density.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Established operators already provide much of the downstream stack, while an industry operator characterizes treatment as high-volume and low-return and reports unresolved second-hand PV guidance; together this directly challenges both intermediary differentiation and wide-margin assumptions.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A narrow multi-installer pilot should produce signed first-notice and title-transfer terms, an activity-specific Polish legal opinion, binding partner and insurance quotes, and a serial-level cohort showing removal volume, product-versus-waste share, buyer bids, realized sale-through, returns, full landed contribution margin, repeat use, and acquisition payback. Results should be reported separately for one equipment class and compared with the incumbent disposal route.
highest_value_structural_change: Narrow the first offer to one high-value, professionally resold equipment class in one dense region and sell installers a contracted, paid pre-removal chain-of-custody and compliant-routing service. Obtain serial data and a contingent professional buyer bid before pickup, accept resale exposure only when the bid covers every landed cost, and route all other units directly to authorized operators; this makes baseline revenue independent of speculative salvage while preserving upside and supply data.
